Chapter 7: Review and Practice

Testing a hypothesis

  • Last week we talked about ways to determine the probability of some an error of a given size and identify a confidence interval around an estimate

  • This week: hypothesis testing

Review: Null hypothesis significance testing

In a previous class, we used an experiment to examine a hypothesis about the ability to distinguish tap water from bottled.

In that test, we had a pair of hypotheses like this:

  • Alternative/Research hypothesis (\(H_a\)): the subject can tell whether a cup contains bottled water or tap water.

  • Null hypothesis \(H_0\): the subject can’t tell, and they’re just guessing.

We used Fisher’s exact test to determine the probability of guessing \(N\) cups correctly if the null hypothesis were true.

We’ll see how this same basic logic can be extended to questions about a sample average or proportion.

Review: Type I and II error

When trying to make a judgement about \(H_0\), there are two ways to be wrong:

  • Type I errors: we think X and Y are related, but the result is actually random. Incorrectly rejecting the null (False positive)

  • Type II errors: X and Y are actually related, but we fail to spot it. Incorrectly failing to reject the null (False negative)

X and Y actually are related X and Y are unrelated
Test is significant Correct Type I error
Test is not significant Type II error Correct

We try to choose methods that minimize the chances of a Type I error

Review: Null vs. Alternative Hypothesis

There are really two “sides” of our hypothesis:

Alternative/Research hypothesis (\(H_a\)): “X and Y are related”, “X influences Y”, or “this outcome is not random”

Null hypothesis \(H_0\): “no relationship”, “no effect” or “no better than random chance”

Technically, we don’t really test \(H_a\). Instead we’ll try to rule out \(H_0\) by asking “how likely is it that random chance would give us results like these?”.

If \(H_0\), we’ll reject the null and say our result is statistically significant. If our test finds \(H_0\) is still plausible, we’ll fail to reject the null and say our result is not statistically significant.

Review: P-Values and null hypothesis testing

The basic framework:

  • Step 1: State a null hypothesis and a significance level (\(\alpha\))

  • Step 2: Assume the null hypothesis is true and ask “What is the probability that random chance would give me a result at least this far away from \(H_0\)?” (P-value)

  • Step 3: If the P-value is less than \(\alpha\) you can reject the null.

Confidence Intervals and null hypothesis testing

  • Step 1: State a null hypothesis and a confidence level

  • Step 2: Calculate a confidence interval for your estimate, and ask: does a confidence interval at this confidence level contain the value assumed under the null hypothesis?

  • Step 3: If the confidence interval doesn’t contain the null hypothesis, you can reject the null.

Tests for a single proportion

In the past, polls have found that a majority of the public opposed abolishing ICE.

However, this may have changed in the last few months, particularly in the wake of two high profile shootings of U.S. citizens by ICE/CBP agents.

Alternative hypothesis (\(H_a\)): Support for abolishing ICE is greater than 50% (\(\rho_{\text{support} \gt .50}\))

Null hypothesis \(H_0\): Support for abolishing ICE is less than or equal to 50% (\(\rho_{\text{support} \leq .50}\))

Tests for a single proportion

Imagine we took a survey of 1,500 people to settle this question, and we decide that we’ll reject the null hypothesis of our p.value is less than .05

Before we look at any data, we have everything we need to visualize the sampling distribution when the population proportion is 50% (which would be a “best case” scenario for the null hypothesis) at this sample size.

Tests for a single proportion

  • The mean of the hypothetical sampling distribution is \(=.5\)
  • The standard error is \(\sqrt{.5(1-.5)/1500} = 0.013\)

Tests for a single proportion

Imagine I draw my sample, and support for abolishing ICE is 51%. What’s the probability of a result at least this high under the null?

Tests for a single proportion

To calculate this, we’ll need to get a Z-score for the difference between our observed sample proportion and the proportion under the null.

\[ \begin{align} Z &= \frac{p - \rho_0}{SE_{\rho_0}} \\ p &= \text{sample proportion} \\ \rho_0 &= \text{hypothetized proportion under the null hypothesis} \\ SE_{\rho_0} &= \text{the standard error of the null proportion} \end{align} \]

Plugging in our values we get:

\[ Z = \frac{.51 - .50}{0.013} = 0.769 \]

Confidence Intervals and null hypothesis testing

\[ Z = \frac{.51 - .50}{0.013} = 0.769 \]

pnorm(0.769, 
      lower.tail=FALSE) # lower tail = FALSE to get probability >= Z
[1] 0.2209467

Tests for a single proportion

What value would I need to see before I rejected the null hypothesis at the .05 level?

  • We’ll reject the null when our sample statistic is in the region where \(P<.05\)

  • In terms of Z-scores, this is when the sample statistic is greater than 1.64 standard errors above 50%.

  • \(0.013 \times 1.645 = 0.021\) above \(.50\) or \(.521\) (\(52.1\%\))

Confidence Intervals and null hypothesis testing

Note that value needed to reach p<.05 will grow or shrink depending on my sample size, even for the same null hypothesis:

Sample size SE Value where p<.05
50 0.07 .62
100 0.05 .58
500 0.02 .54
1500 0.01 .52
5000 <0.01 .51

Confidence Intervals and null hypothesis testing

Confidence Intervals and null hypothesis testing

  • Note that we specified a directional hypothesis about the proportion of people who support abolishing ICE.

  • What if we don’t have a directional hypothesis?

Confidence Intervals and null hypothesis testing

  • In a survey of 1,316 adults, 76% of respondents in a sample said they voted in the 2024 election.

  • In the 2024 election, adult turnout was estimated closer to 59%.

  • So what is the probability of getting an error of \(\pm17\) in a sample with 1,316 people?

A one sample test of proportions

  • In a survey of 1,316 adults, 76% of respondents in a sample said they voted in the 2024 election.

  • In the 2024 election, adult turnout was 59%.

  • My null hypothesis is that this is a random sample from the adult population, and so the true population value should be 59%. Can I reject this at the .05 level?

A one sample test of proportions

  • The percent turnout under the null hypothesis is \(59\%\)
  • So, we just want to calculate the probability of being off by \(17\) percentage points in either direction.
  • \(\text{SE} = \sqrt{\frac{76 \times (100-76)}{1316}} \approx 1.2\)
  • \(Z = \frac{17}{1.2} \approx 14.2\)

A one sample test of proportions

testpropsC(x1= survey$voted24, x2 = .59, response='Yes')

  • What is the probability of seeing a result this extreme if the null is true (look the p-value)?

  • Is the result statistically significant at the .05 level?

A one sample test of proportions: confidence interval method

The confidence interval method will give us the same result here. Instead of looking for a p-value less than alpha, we can ask “does the confidence interval for the difference contain zero”?

  • .05 significance in a two-tailed test is equivalent to a 95% confidence interval.

  • The Z-score associated with a 95% confidence interval is about 1.96

  • \(.17 \pm 1.96 \times 1.2 \approx [.145, .191]\)

Sample error

  • Why is our sample so different from the population?

  • How does this change our interpretation of hypothesis tests?

Two sample proportions

  • Consider this result from a recent YouGov survey on attitudes about the Middle Ages. N = 2,230

  • (Note that YouGov used an online opt-in panel here, which should lead us to be a little more skeptical about the reliability of these estimates, but we can set this aside for now)

Two sample proportions

  • Can we rule out the hypothesis that the Inquisition and the Black Plague are equally popular? Is this difference statistically significant at the .05 level?

  • \(H_0 =\) People are equally favorable towards both (the difference = 0)

  • \(H_a =\) The Plague and the Inquisition are not equally popular (the difference does not = 0)

Two sample proportions

  • Calculate the observed difference: \(0.16 - 0.09 = .07\)

  • Calculate the standard error of the difference: \(\text{SE}_\text{diff}=\sqrt{\frac{.16\times(1-.16)}{2,230} + \frac{0.09 \times (1-0.09)}{2,230}} \approx .01\)

  • Calculate the Z score: \(.07/.01 = 7\)

Two sample proportions

testpropsC(x1 = inquisition, x2=plague, response='favorable', data=yougov_data, printC=TRUE)

  • What is the probability of seeing a difference at least this large if there is no difference between evaluations of the Plague and the Inquisition?

  • Can we reject the null hypothesis at the .05 level?

  • What would change here if our hypothesis was that the Inquisition was more popular than the Plague? What if we hypothesized that the Plague was more popular than the Inquisition?

Two sample proportions: confidence interval method

Again: the confidence interval method will give us the same result here. Instead of looking for a p-value less .05 we can ask “does the 95% confidence interval for the difference contain zero”?

What to use when

  • For categorical by categorical relationships: use a \(\chi^2\) test. (crosstabC with chisq=TRUE)

  • To compare a sample mean to a hypothetical value, or compare the averages for two groups, use a difference of means test. (testsPropC)

  • To compare a sample proportion to a hypothetical value, or compare the proportions from two groups, use a difference of proportions test.(testMeansC)

Cautions about hypothesis testing

How not to use a p-value

How not to use a p-value

  • Charles Cicchetti, writing in a deposition for the plaintiffs in a lawsuit claiming mass vote fraud swung the 2020 election, used a difference of proportion test to compare Biden’s 2020 results in Georgia to Clinton’s results in the same state.

  • The goal was to “test the hypothesis that other things being equal they would have an equal number of votes”

How not to use a p-value

Clinton’s 2016 vote \(= 45.9\%\) with \(4,146,825\) total votes cast

Biden’s 2020 vote \(= 49.5\%\) with \(4,999,960\) total votes cast

\[ \text{diff} = .495 - .459 = .036 \]

\[ \text{SE}_{\text{diff}} = \sqrt{\frac{.459 \times (1 - .459)}{4146825} + \frac{.495 \times (1-.495)}{4999960}} = 0.000331 \]

\[ Z = \frac{.036}{0.000331} = 108.7 \]

\[ P |Z| > z \approx 1 \text{ in } 1,000,000,000,000,000 \]

How not to use a p-value

“In my opinion, the outcome of Biden winning is so statistically improbable, that it is not possible to dismiss fraud and biased changes in the ways ballots were processed, validated, and tabulated” - Charles Cicchetti

The math checks out! So what’s wrong with this claim?

What is the null hypothesis in this case? What can we conclude from rejecting it?

How not to use a p-value

if the objective is to assess whether Biden won legitimately, then it is beside the point whether Biden and Clinton enjoyed the same expected support. Support can differ across candidates for any number of reasons, and it is absurd to think that any such difference constitutes evidence of election fraud. -Eggers, Garro, and Grimmer

(the authors go on to note that they can reject this null in every state in every presidential election since 1960)

This tells us that differences across elections aren’t random, but that’s probably not the most important question for researchers!

What hypothesis testing does

In experimental research, “treatment” is randomly assigned, so once we’ve eliminated “random chance”, we can conclude the difference is due to the treatment.

What hypothesis testing does

  • In observational research, ruling out random chance is just the first step towards identifying a cause
  • We’d need to rule out a lot of other more plausible explanations here first.

P-hacking and the “replication crisis”

P-hacking and the “replication crisis”

Lots of causes, but bad hypothesis testing plays a role:

  • P < .05 means “1 in 20 results will be a Type I error”

  • So, what happens if I just test everything?

P-hacking and the “replication crisis”

Here’s a function that produces random results, runs a t-test, and then determines whether the results are significant at the .05 level:

set.seed(100)

simulate_experiment<-function(){
  N <- 100
  treatment_assignment<-rep(c("control group", "test group"), each = N/2)
  outcome<-rnorm(length(treatment_assignment))
  p<-t.test(outcome ~ treatment_assignment)$p.value
  significance <- ifelse(p < .05, "significant", "not significant")
  return(significance)
}

P-hacking and the “replication crisis”

If I run this function 100 times, I’ll get about 5 significant results:

p_values<-replicate(n=100, expr = simulate_experiment())
barplot(table(p_values), main = "Significance tests for 100 simulated experiments")

but there’s definitely not a relationship here. This is random noise!

P-hacking and the “replication crisis”

  • The ANES has thousands of variables, so there are bound to be hundreds of combinations that will give us significant results purely by chance.

  • P-hacking, or trying out a bunch of models until one just gets over the threshold for significance, is bound to produce false positives.

P-hacking and the “replication crisis”

  • In published research, there are few incentives to publish a non-significant result, so people sometimes run lots of tests and only publish the ones that “work”

  • Which results in lots of findings that later can’t be replicated: they were just random false positives.

Best practices

  • Exploring your data is fine (especially when you’re learning) but running more tests means you should be more skeptical of your results.

  • As a reader, you should be cautious when you see a result that just barely meets the criteria for significance, especially if its:

    • Not supported by additional replications or the hypothesis wasn’t pre-registered

    • Un-intuitive or not based on some pre-existing theory or reasonable expectation

    • Substantively small and/or based on a small sample

Difference of Two Means

Difference of Two Means

  • \(\text{diff} = -.68\)

  • \(\text{SE}_\text{diff} = \sqrt{\frac{2.33^2}{796} + \frac{2.57^2}{498}} \approx{0.142}\)

  • \(\text{T} = \frac{.68}{0.142} = 4.8\)

  • (The T distribution is going to be very similar to a Z distribution because our N is over 30.)
